s: What is the maximum penalty that can be imposed on a PIO under Section 20 of the RTI Act?
x: The penalty is ₹250 per day up to a maximum of ₹25,000, after a hearing.

s: Under Section 19 of the RTI Act, within how many days does a second appeal to the CIC or SIC lie?
x: The first appeal lies within the public authority; the second appeal goes to the CIC/SIC within 90 days.

s: Which of the following pairs of RTI Act Section and content is correctly matched?
x: Section 18 deals with complaints; Section 12 constitutes the CIC, Section 5 designates PIOs and Section 20 is the penalty.

s: Which body alone can declare an organisation a 'public authority' under the RTI Act?
x: The CIC is the only body that can declare an organisation a public authority.

s: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 amended which provision of the RTI Act?
x: The DPDP Act, 2023 amended Section 8(1)(j) on personal information.

s: Before the 2019 amendment, the pay of a State Chief Information Commissioner was equal to that of which office?
x: Earlier, the State Chief IC's pay equalled an Election Commissioner's pay.

s: Under Section 7 of the RTI Act, within how many days must information ordinarily be supplied?
x: Section 7 requires a reply within 30 days; 48 hours where life or liberty is involved.

s: Under Section 7 of the RTI Act, which applicants are not charged any fee for information?
x: Section 7 of the RTI Act says no fee is charged from persons below the poverty line.

s: Which of the following describes the Anti-Corruption Bureau in Andhra Pradesh?
o: A Union agency operating only under the FEMA
A State police agency dealing with offences under the Prevention of Corruption Act
A statutory commission appointed by the President
A judicial body hearing appeals against the State Vigilance Commission
x: The Andhra Pradesh ACB is a State police agency that deals with offences under the Prevention of Corruption Act.

s: In which year was the State Vigilance Commission of Andhra Pradesh set up?
x: The AP State Vigilance Commission dates from 1964.

s:
Consider the following statements about anti-corruption bodies in Andhra Pradesh:
1. The Anti-Corruption Bureau is a State police agency for Prevention of Corruption Act offences.
2. The State Vigilance Commission took over part of the State Public Service Commission's disciplinary role.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Both are correct: the ACB handles PC Act offences, and the 1964 Vigilance Commission took over part of the SPSC's disciplinary role.

s: Through which of the following was the Planning Commission set up on 15 March 1950?
x: The Planning Commission was set up by a Cabinet resolution and was neither constitutional nor statutory.

s: On which date did the Union Cabinet repeal the 1950 resolution that created the Planning Commission?
x: The Cabinet repealed the resolution on 13 August 2014, and NITI Aayog replaced the Commission.

s: Through which of the following was the National Development Council set up on 6 August 1952?
x: The NDC was set up by executive order; it linked the Planning Commission and the States.

s: Who was the first Chairman of the Planning Commission?
x: The Prime Minister chaired the Planning Commission; its first chairman was Jawaharlal Nehru (1950).

s: The Planning Commission was abolished in 2014 during the tenure of which Prime Minister?
x: The Modi government's Cabinet repealed the 1950 resolution on 13 August 2014 and set up NITI Aayog.

s: Who among the following was NOT a member of the National Development Council?
x: The NDC had the PM, all State CMs and Planning Commission members; the CJI was not a member.

s: The National Development Council was restructured into which body of NITI Aayog?
x: The NDC (PM, all State CMs, Planning Commission members) was restructured into NITI's Governing Council.

s: In the Governing Council of NITI Aayog, who represents Union Territories without legislatures?
x: The Governing Council includes CMs of UTs with legislatures and Lieutenant Governors of the other UTs.

s: Who chairs the Regional Councils of NITI Aayog?
o: Chief Minister of the largest State in the region
Lieutenant Governor of a Union Territory in the region
x: Regional Councils are chaired by the PM or his nominee; CMs and LGs of the region are members.

s: SETUs, supported by NITI Aayog under the State Support Mission, are meant to help States prepare which of the following?
x: NITI Aayog assists States in setting up State Economic and Transformation Units, or SETUs, to prepare State Vision@2047 plans.

s: Which NITI Aayog vertical leads the engagement of States with the Centre?
x: The Team India Hub is responsible for leading engagement between the States and the Centre.

s: Which body is now the nodal agency for poverty estimation in India?
x: NITI Aayog (earlier the Planning Commission) is the nodal agency for poverty estimation and also brings out the National MPI. The Finance Commission, RBI and Rural Development Ministry are not the nodal agency.

s: Which of the following describes NITI Aayog, set up on 1 January 2015?
o: A statutory body set up by an Act of Parliament
A think-tank set up by a Union Cabinet resolution
A body under the Finance Commission
x: NITI Aayog was set up by a Cabinet resolution and is neither constitutional nor statutory.

s: Who replaced Suman K. Bery as Vice-Chairperson of NITI Aayog in 2026?
x: Ashok Kumar Lahiri replaced Suman K. Bery by an order of 25 April 2026.

s: What rank do the full-time members of NITI Aayog hold?
o: Secretary to the Government of India
x: Full-time members have Minister of State rank; the Vice-Chairperson has Cabinet rank.

s: Which NITI Aayog hub builds its think-tank capacity?
x: The Knowledge and Innovation Hub builds think-tank capacity; the Team India Hub handles States-Centre engagement.

s: When was NITI Aayog set up?
x: NITI Aayog was set up on 1 January 2015 by a Union Cabinet resolution.

s: What rank does the Vice-Chairperson of NITI Aayog hold?
o: Secretary to the Government of India
x: The Vice-Chairperson, the executive head of NITI Aayog, holds Cabinet rank; full-time members hold MoS rank.

s: Which of the following is true of NITI Aayog, unlike the Planning Commission?
o: Was set up by an Act of Parliament
Does not allocate funds to States
x: NITI Aayog has no fund-allocation role, which lies with the Finance Ministry and the Finance Commission.

s: How is NITI Aayog's approach to planning described?
o: Bottom-up, based on fund allocation to States
x: NITI follows a bottom-up approach of cooperative federalism (Team India), unlike the Planning Commission's top-down one.

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Planning Commission followed a top-down approach to planning.
2. Both the Planning Commission and NITI Aayog were set up by Cabinet resolutions.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Both are correct: the Planning Commission was top-down, and both bodies rest on Cabinet resolutions (1950 and 2015).

s: In the 4th edition (2023-24) of NITI Aayog's SDG India Index, Andhra Pradesh
o: scored 74 and was placed in the 'Front Runner' category
was not ranked because it used only 49 indicators
x: The 2023-24 edition (released July 2024) used 113 indicators; AP scored 74 and was a 'Front Runner'. The other options give wrong scores or categories, and 49 is the ADP indicator count, not the SDG Index's.

s: What does the SDG India Index primarily measure?
o: States’ progress towards Sustainable Development Goals
Multidimensional poverty through only health indicators
x: The SDG India Index assesses the progress of States and Union Territories towards the Sustainable Development Goals.

s: What was Andhra Pradesh's rank in the Export Preparedness Index 2024, released in January 2026?
x: Andhra Pradesh was ranked fifth among large States in the Export Preparedness Index 2024.

s: Which one of the following is correctly matched?
o: India Electric Mobility Index — Agricultural poverty
Export Preparedness Index — States’ export readiness
School Education Quality Index — Export competitiveness
x: The Export Preparedness Index assesses States' export readiness. The India Electric Mobility Index measures e-mobility across States, the GROW report concerns Greening and Restoration of Wasteland with Agroforestry, and the School Education Quality Index concerns school education, so the other pairs are wrong.

s: What is the subject of the GROW report of NITI Aayog?
o: Groundwater Recharge and Optimal Water use
Greening and Restoration of Wasteland with Agroforestry
x: GROW stands for Greening and Restoration of Wasteland with Agroforestry.

s: How many indicators does the National Multidimensional Poverty Index use?
x: The National MPI uses 12 indicators, including maternal health and bank account, over the Global MPI base.

s: According to the National MPI, what was Andhra Pradesh's multidimensional poverty in 2019-21?
x: AP fell from 11.77% to 6.06%; India fell from 24.85% to 14.96%.

s: With which institution does NITI Aayog prepare the Export Preparedness Index?
x: The EPI, first released in 2020, is prepared with the Institute for Competitiveness.

s: Which of the following indicators was added in India's National Multidimensional Poverty Index over the Global MPI base?
x: India's National MPI uses 12 indicators, adding maternal health and bank account to the Global MPI base.

s: According to the National MPI, what share of India's population was multidimensionally poor in 2019-21?
x: National MPI fell from 24.85% (2015-16) to 14.96% (2019-21).

s: How many indicators were used in the 4th edition (2023-24) of NITI Aayog's SDG India Index?
x: The 4th edition (2023-24) of the SDG India Index used 113 indicators.

s: With which organisation did NITI Aayog bring out the India Electric Mobility Index?
x: NITI Aayog prepares the India Electric Mobility Index with WRI India; the EPI is with the Institute for Competitiveness.

s: In NITI Aayog's SDG India Index, Andhra Pradesh ranked first in which Goal?
x: Andhra Pradesh is 1st in SDG 7 and 2nd in SDG 14.

s: Which institution runs the Aspirational Districts Programme?
x: The Aspirational Districts Programme is run by NITI Aayog.

s: What is the coverage of the Aspirational Blocks Programme launched in January 2023?
o: 329 blocks in 513 districts across all States
513 districts in 329 blocks across 27 States and 4 Union Territories
513 blocks in 329 districts across 27 States and 4 Union Territories
x: The Aspirational Blocks Programme, launched in January 2023, covers 513 blocks in 329 districts across 27 States and 4 Union Territories.

s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Atal Innovation Mission — Innovation and entrepreneurship
Women Entrepreneurship Platform — Monthly delta ranking of districts
Aspirational Blocks Programme — Five-Year Plan approval
Sampoornata Abhiyan 2.0 — Appointment of NITI Aayog CEO
x: The Atal Innovation Mission promotes innovation and entrepreneurship through initiatives such as Atal Tinkering Labs and incubators.

s: Which one of the following is NOT one of the five themes of the Aspirational Districts Programme?
x: The five themes include Health and Nutrition, Education, Agriculture and Water Resources, Financial Inclusion and Skill Development, and Basic Infrastructure. Urban Transport and Housing is not listed as a theme.

s: What is the coverage of the Aspirational Districts Programme, launched in January 2018?
o: 112 districts using 49 indicators across five themes
112 districts using 49 indicators across ten themes
x: The Aspirational Districts Programme was launched in January 2018 and covers 112 districts, using 49 indicators grouped under five themes.

s: The strategy of the Aspirational Districts Programme is based on which of the following?
x: The programme uses the three-dimensional strategy of Convergence, Collaboration and Competition.

s: Which of the following districts constituted the original group of Aspirational Districts in Andhra Pradesh?
x: The original aspirational districts of Andhra Pradesh were Vizianagaram, Visakhapatnam and YSR Kadapa.

s: What weight does Financial Inclusion and Skill Development carry under the Aspirational Districts Programme?
x: Financial Inclusion and Skill Development carries 10 percent; Agriculture and Water Resources carries 20 percent.

s: Which of the following is the current set of Aspirational Districts of Andhra Pradesh mentioned for the 2025-26 State Survey?
o: Alluri Sitarama Raju, Parvathipuram Manyam and YSR Kadapa
x: The current set mentioned is Alluri Sitarama Raju, Parvathipuram Manyam and YSR Kadapa. Vizianagaram and Visakhapatnam belong to the earlier list, while Kurnool and Anantapur are not included in the current set.

s: Regarding the seven backward districts of Andhra Pradesh under the AP Reorganisation Act, 2014, which pair is correctly matched?
x: The seven backward districts are 4 in Rayalaseema and 3 in North Coastal Andhra.

s: In which year was the Atal Innovation Mission launched?
x: The Atal Innovation Mission (2016) runs Atal Tinkering Labs and incubators.

s: Which of the following pairs of NITI Aayog initiative and launch year is correctly matched?
x: The WEP began in 2018; ADP is January 2018, ABP January 2023 and AIM 2016.

s: Which of the following is NOT an Aspirational District of Andhra Pradesh?
x: Kurnool and Anantapur are not AP aspirational districts; the others are in the original or current list.

s: What weight does the Health and Nutrition theme carry under the Aspirational Districts Programme?
x: Health and Nutrition carries 30%; Agriculture and Water Resources 20%; Financial Inclusion and Basic Infrastructure 10% each.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the forms of decentralisation?
o: Delegation transfers powers to elected local governments with their own revenue
Deconcentration shifts work to field offices of the same government
Delegation entrusts tasks to semi-autonomous bodies
Devolution transfers powers to elected local governments with their own mandate and revenue
x: Delegation entrusts tasks to semi-autonomous bodies; transferring powers to elected local governments with their own mandate and revenue is devolution.

s: Judicial review, unlike public health, sanitation and water supply, is a function of which of the following?
x: Public health, sanitation and water supply are local functions; judicial review belongs to the higher courts.

s: Which dimension of decentralisation transfers the power to spend and raise funds and taxes?
x: Fiscal decentralisation concerns spending and raising funds and taxes; political concerns deciding, administrative concerns implementing.

s: Which one of the following is NOT a feature of decentralisation?
x: Autonomy, people's participation and empowerment of local communities are features of decentralisation. Instilling non-confidence among local communities is not a feature.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Local accountability – decisions at the apex
Local Self-Government – exercise in democratic decentralisation
x: Local self-government is democratic decentralisation because it brings community participation and local accountability.

s: The power to take back an entrusted authority at will is the decisive test distinguishing which of the following?
x: If the transferring authority can withdraw the power at will, the arrangement is delegation rather than devolution. Devolved powers are not ordinarily withdrawable at will by the transferring authority.

s: What is the shifting of work to field offices of the same government, with the Centre keeping full control, called?
x: Deconcentration moves work to field offices of the same government and is the weakest form.

s: Which form of decentralisation, given effect by the 73rd and 74th Amendments, is the strongest?
x: Devolution gives powers to elected local governments with their own mandate and revenue, not withdrawable at will.

s:
Consider the following statements about decentralisation:
1. Political decentralisation transfers the power to decide to elected local bodies.
2. Administrative decentralisation transfers the power to implement through staff and functions.
3. Deconcentration is the strongest form of decentralisation.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct; deconcentration is the weakest form, devolution the strongest.

s: Which of the following is NOT a function of local government?
x: Public health, sanitation and rural development are local functions; public order is not.

s: Which of the following represents the Gandhian conception of village self-government?
o: A centralised planned state based on heavy industry
A republic of self-sufficient villages with decentralised economic and political power
A system of village administration controlled by departmental headquarters
A local-government system limited to implementation of centrally prepared plans
x: Gandhi advocated Gram Swaraj, conceived as a republic of self-sufficient villages with decentralised economic and political power.

s: Which of the following did the Nehruvian approach to state and development favour?
o: A centralised planned state with heavy industry
Cottage industries as the basis of planning
Complete fiscal autonomy for village panchayats
x: Nehru favoured a centralised planned state with heavy industry (National Planning Committee, Bombay Plan); self-sufficient villages were Gandhi's idea.

s: On 4 November 1948, B.R. Ambedkar described the Indian village as which of the following?
o: The primary constitutional unit protected from all central authority
A seat of caste domination and a sink of localism, ignorance, narrow-mindedness and communalism
A model of decentralised economic and political power
x: Ambedkar criticised the village as a seat of caste domination and called it a sink of localism, a den of ignorance, narrow-mindedness and communalism on 4 November 1948.

s: With whom is the Gandhian Plan of 1944 associated?
x: Sriman Narayan Agarwal drew up the Gandhian Plan (1944).

s: For B.R. Ambedkar, what was to be the unit of the Constitution?
x: Ambedkar saw the village as a seat of caste domination and made the individual the unit.

s: Who described the Indian village as 'a sink of localism, a den of ignorance, narrow-mindedness and communalism'?
x: B.R. Ambedkar said this in the Constituent Assembly on 4 November 1948.

s: Article 40, on organising village panchayats, belongs to which of the following categories?
x: Article 40 is a Directive Principle in Part IV; it is non-justiciable.

s: Article 40 is generally regarded as a compromise between which two perspectives?
o: The Gandhian advocacy of panchayats and Ambedkar's reservations about the village
The Union List and the State List
The Nehruvian advocacy of heavy industry and the Gandhian advocacy of cottage industry
x: Article 40 represented a compromise: panchayats were named as an objective, reflecting the Gandhian position, but the provision was made non-justiciable, accommodating Ambedkar's reservations.

s: Why did the 64th Amendment Bill of 1989 fail to become law?
o: It passed the Lok Sabha but failed in the Rajya Sabha amid fears of centralisation
It was rejected by the Supreme Court for violating Article 40
It failed to secure passage in the Lok Sabha because it opposed decentralisation
It lapsed because the State legislatures refused to ratify it unanimously
x: The 64th Amendment Bill, associated with Rajiv Gandhi, passed the Lok Sabha but failed in the Rajya Sabha because of fears that it would promote centralisation.

s: Which Articles, giving Article 40 practical shape, came with the 73rd Amendment?
x: The 73rd Amendment gave Article 40 practical shape through Articles 243A, 243B and 243G.

s: Which Article of the Constitution directs the State to organise Village Panchayats as units of self-government?
x: Article 40, a Directive Principle, tells the State to organise village panchayats as units of self-government. Articles 243A, 243B and 243G came much later with the 73rd Amendment.

s: Which of the following is true of Article 40, which directs the State to organise village panchayats?
o: Part of Part IX of the Constitution
Parliament's power to modify Fundamental Rights
x: Article 40 is a Directive Principle in Part IV and is non-justiciable; Article 33 concerns modifying Fundamental Rights.

s: In India's decentralisation experience, which power was transferred the least to local governments?
x: India transferred political power, some administrative power and the least fiscal power - the decentralisation gap.

s: Despite favouring a centralised planned state, where and when did Jawaharlal Nehru inaugurate Panchayati Raj?
x: Nehru inaugurated Panchayati Raj at Nagaur in Rajasthan on 2 October 1959. Andhra Pradesh followed on 1 November 1959; 1952 is the Community Development Programme year; January 1957 is when the Balwant Rai Mehta Committee was appointed.

s: Which of the following illustrates historical village autonomy in the Andhra Pradesh region?
o: The Solid Waste Management Rules, 2026 under Article 253
The 12-Ayagar village administration associated with the Kakatiyas and Vijayanagara
The transfer of all local functions to the Union Government
The Justice Kurian Joseph committee on Union-State relations
x: The traditional 12-Ayagar village administration under the Kakatiyas and Vijayanagara is cited as an example of historical village autonomy in the Andhra region.

s: When was the Balwant Rai Mehta Committee, set up after the top-down CDP, appointed?
x: The CDP (1952) ran top-down; the Balwant Rai Mehta Committee was appointed in January 1957.

s: Which was the second State to introduce Panchayati Raj, on 1 November 1959?
x: After Rajasthan (Nagaur, 2 October 1959), Andhra Pradesh introduced Panchayati Raj on 1 November 1959.

s: Which of the following was an argument advanced in favour of centralisation in India after Independence?
o: Local bodies possess complete knowledge of local needs
Nation-building after Partition required unity and security
x: Nation-building after Partition, along with the requirements of unity and security, was an argument for centralisation. The other options are arguments for decentralisation.

s: In India, the risk of elite capture by locally dominant castes was cited as an argument for which of the following?
x: Elite capture by dominant local castes was cited in favour of centralisation, not decentralisation.

s: Which of the following was an argument for decentralisation in India?
o: Planned heavy industry needs a single command
Food security needs a single command
x: Proximity to local needs argues for decentralisation; heavy industry, food security and elite capture were arguments for centralisation.

s: Which of the following is NOT an argument for decentralisation?
x: Weak local capacity was an argument for centralisation; the others favour decentralisation.

s: A State has regularly elected local bodies, but they lack adequate funds to perform their assigned functions. Which conclusion most accurately follows from the principle of decentralisation?
o: Without fiscal decentralisation, elected local bodies may remain powerless.
Fiscal decentralisation necessarily eliminates the role of State Governments.
Local bodies become constitutionally invalid if they lack sufficient funds.
Election alone automatically ensures effective local self-government.
x: Political decentralisation through elections is insufficient by itself. Local bodies require fiscal decentralisation and adequate financial powers to exercise their responsibilities effectively.

s: Which one of the following correctly describes the principle of subsidiarity?
o: Every function must be performed by the Union Government for uniformity
Local bodies may perform only those functions expressly delegated temporarily by the Centre
A function should be performed at the lowest level competent to do so and move upward only when that level cannot perform it
The highest tier should decide all functions and lower tiers should implement them
x: Subsidiarity assigns a function to the lowest competent level and permits movement to a higher level only when the lower level cannot perform it adequately.

s: In the context of Panchayati Raj Institutions, what do the three Fs stand for?
x: The three Fs are Funds, Functions and Functionaries. Effective devolution requires all three rather than merely assigning responsibilities on paper.

s: What is the principal consequence of incomplete devolution of the three Fs to Panchayati Raj Institutions?
o: They remain primarily implementing agencies rather than planning units
They replace the State legislature in rural areas
They become fully autonomous planning governments
They acquire complete control over State taxation
x: Without adequate funds, functions and functionaries, Panchayati Raj Institutions remain implementing agencies instead of becoming effective planning units.

s: Under the principle of subsidiarity, when does a function move to a higher level?
o: The Centre decides to withdraw it
The lowest competent level cannot perform it
Funds are not available at the district
x: Subsidiarity places a function at the lowest competent level; it moves up only if that level cannot do it.

s: Which body invoked the principle of subsidiarity for local government?
x: The 2nd ARC invoked subsidiarity: functions at the lowest competent level.

s: Local self-government can be explained as an exercise in which of the following?
x: UPSC 2017 keyed 'democratic decentralisation': power is transferred to elected local bodies. Federalism is about Union-State division; delegation can be withdrawn at will; direct democracy is citizens deciding without representatives.

s: Panchayati Raj Institutions brought which significant change in village governance?
o: Abolition of local participation in development
Direct control by Parliament over village decisions
x: PRIs brought formal representation of weaker sections in village governance and were adopted to decentralise democratic power.

s: Which committee coined the term 'democratic decentralisation'?
x: The Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957) coined the term, not the Ashok Mehta Committee.

s: What is the system in which citizens decide matters without representatives called?
x: Direct democracy means citizens decide without representatives; democratic decentralisation passes power to elected local bodies.

s: Along with democratic decentralisation, which was a fundamental objective of Panchayati Raj?
x: The fundamental objectives were people's participation in development and democratic decentralisation; financial mobilisation was not one.

s: After the 73rd Amendment, effective Panchayati Raj needs decentralisation of decision-making, of administrative powers and of what else?
x: The needs identified are decentralisation of decision-making, administrative powers and the system as a whole - not judicial powers.

s: Who is known as the 'Father of Local Self-Government in India'?
x: Lord Ripon, through his 1882 resolution, is the father of local self-government; Lord Mayo's 1870 resolution was about financial decentralisation.

s: With which of the following is Lord Mayo's resolution of 1870 associated?
o: Elected non-official majorities in local boards
x: Mayo's 1870 resolution gave financial decentralisation, mainly for fiscal relief; elected non-official majorities came with Ripon.

s: On which date was Lord Ripon's Resolution on Local Self-Government issued?
x: Ripon's resolution of 18 May 1882 treated local bodies as instruments of political and popular education.

s: From which pattern does India's municipal model, through Ripon's boards, come?
x: India's municipal model derives from the British pattern of Ripon's boards.

s: Lord Ripon's Resolution of 1882 treated local bodies mainly as instruments of which of the following?
x: Ripon's 1882 resolution saw local bodies as instruments of political and popular education; Mayo's 1870 resolution was about finance.

s: Which Viceroy's resolution provided for elected non-official majorities and non-official chairmen in local boards?
x: Lord Ripon's resolution of 18 May 1882 provided elected non-official majorities and non-official chairmen.

s: Which one of the following is NOT a feature of local self-government?
o: Election by and accountability to local people
A defined local area and functions
x: Local self-government does not possess sovereignty or legislative supremacy. Its features include local accountability, defined functions, own funds and autonomy within State law.

s: To whom do sovereignty and legislative supremacy, which are not features of local self-government, belong?
x: Sovereignty and legislative supremacy belong to Parliament and State legislatures, never to local bodies.

s:
Consider the following statements about local self-government:
1. It has a defined local area and functions.
2. It enjoys autonomy within State law.
3. It exercises judicial powers.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Defined area and functions and autonomy within State law are features; judicial powers are not (Nyaya Panchayats are separate).

s: In which Article is the constitutional trace of the idea of Gram Swaraj found?
x: The constitutional trace of Gram Swaraj is found in Article 40, a Directive Principle of State Policy concerning village panchayats.

s: Which Ministry implements the Rashtriya Gram Swaraj Abhiyan, which trains members of Panchayati Raj Institutions?
x: RGSA is implemented by the Ministry of Panchayati Raj from 2018-19 to train PRI members.

s: Whose idea is Gram Swaraj, whose constitutional root is Article 40?
x: Gram Swaraj is Gandhi's self-reliant village republic; Article 40 is its constitutional root.

s: Under the revamped Rashtriya Gram Swaraj Abhiyan, what is the Centre-State funding ratio for North-Eastern and hill States?
x: RGSA funding is 60:40, and 90:10 for NE and hill States.

s: What is the Centre-State funding ratio for general States under the revamped Rashtriya Gram Swaraj Abhiyan?
x: RGSA is funded 60:40 by the Centre and States; North-Eastern and hill States get 90:10.

s: From which year has the Rashtriya Gram Swaraj Abhiyan, which trains PRI members, been implemented?
x: RGSA runs from 2018-19; it was revamped for 1 April 2022 to 31 March 2026.

s: Which committee recommended constitutional status for Panchayati Raj Institutions, which the Balwant Rai Mehta Committee did not?
x: Balwant Rai Mehta sought a three-tier system, genuine transfer of power and adequate resources; constitutional status came with the L.M. Singhvi Committee.

s: What did the Ashok Mehta Committee recommend about the supersession of a local body?
o: Elections should be held only after five years of supersession
There should be no supersession, or elections should be held within six months
Supersession could continue indefinitely without elections
Supersession should be decided by the Union Cabinet
x: The committee recommended no supersession, or that polls should be conducted within six months if supersession occurred.

s: The expression “grass without roots” was used in the context of which observation?
o: Development had become bureaucratised, requiring restoration of the Zila Parishad’s role
Municipal corporations had become financially autonomous
Village communities had acquired excessive judicial powers
x: The G.V.K. Rao Committee observed that development had become bureaucratised—described as “grass without roots”—and called for restoration of the Zila Parishad’s role.

s:
The Committee on Policy and Programmes (1988) recommended which of the following?
1. Constitutional status for PRIs
2. A five-year term for PRIs
3. State Finance Commissions and State Election Commissions
x: The 1988 Committee recommended constitutional status, a five-year term, direct elections, and State Finance and Election Commissions.

s: By whom did the Hanumantha Rao Committee (1984) recommend that district planning be coordinated?
x: The Hanumantha Rao Committee wanted the Collector to coordinate district planning.

s: Which committee recommended block-level planning in 1978?
x: The Dantwala Committee (1978) recommended block-level planning. The Hanumantha Rao Committee (1984) recommended district planning with the Collector coordinating it; G.V.K. Rao (1985) spoke of 'grass without roots'; Ashok Mehta (1977-78) made the district the first point of decentralisation.

s: Whose full cooperation did the Balwant Rai Mehta Committee hold necessary for development?
x: The Mehta Committee held local public participation indispensable for development.

s: When did the National Development Council accept the Balwant Rai Mehta Committee's report?
x: The committee reported in 1957 and the NDC accepted it in January 1958.

s: According to the Balwant Rai Mehta Committee, which of the following was needed for democratic decentralisation to succeed?
o: Genuine transfer of power with adequate resources
x: The Mehta Committee called for genuine transfer of power and adequate resources; it did not ask for constitutional status.

s: On which date did Andhra Pradesh follow Rajasthan in introducing Panchayati Raj?
x: Rajasthan inaugurated Panchayati Raj at Nagaur on 2 October 1959; Andhra Pradesh followed on 1 November 1959.

s: Into how many Zilla Parishads are Andhra Pradesh's 13 Zilla Parishads being reorganised in 2026?
x: AP's 13 Zilla Parishads are reorganised into 28, one per district, after their terms ended on 24 September 2026.

s: With which of the following is SabhaSaar, in the context of Gram Sabha functioning, associated?
o: Conduct of elections to Jammu and Kashmir DDCs
Collection of property tax by Zilla Parishads
Preparation of Gram Sabha minutes using an artificial intelligence tool
x: SabhaSaar is an AI tool associated with Gram Sabha minutes.

s: Under which Article is the District Planning Committee constitutionally recognised as a coordinating body?
x: The District Planning Committee is a constitutional coordinating body under Article 243ZD.

s: Which of the following pairs relating to Kerala's People's Plan Campaign is INCORRECTLY matched?
o: People's Plan Campaign 2.0 – T.M. Thomas Isaac
People's Plan Campaign 2.0 – student internships and an online portal
x: About 35-40% of plan funds were devolved, not 60-70%; the other pairs are correct.

s: About what share of plan funds did Kerala's People's Plan Campaign devolve to local bodies?
x: About 35-40% of plan funds were devolved, not 60-70%.

s: Which of the following correctly describes the Scandinavian model of local government?
o: Strong municipalities delivering most welfare services with high local taxes
Local councils functioning only through parliamentary committees
Village bodies exercising judicial supremacy over the State
Weak municipalities dependent mainly on central grants
x: The Scandinavian model is characterised by strong municipalities, delivery of most welfare services and high local taxes; it is treated as a benchmark for fiscal decentralisation.

s: Which one of the following is a characteristic of the British model of local government?
o: Local bodies deliver most welfare services through high local taxes
Municipalities possess complete sovereignty independent of Parliament
Local councils are creatures of Parliament and operate under the ultra vires rule
All local councils are governed through Gram Panchayats
x: In the British model, local councils are creatures of Parliament and are subject to the ultra vires rule; the model also uses a committee system.

s:
Consider the following statements about global models of local government:
1. In the British model, local councils are creatures of Parliament bound by the ultra vires rule.
2. The Scandinavian model, with strong municipalities and high local taxes, is a benchmark for fiscal decentralisation.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Both are correct: British councils are creatures of Parliament under the ultra vires rule; Scandinavian municipalities are the fiscal-decentralisation benchmark.
